stem: A claims agent must post an adjuster decision to a legacy policy system that occasionally acknowledges twice. What belongs in the integration design?

opts.A: Instruct Claude never to submit the same claim twice
opts.B: A caller-supplied idempotency key enforced by the write endpoint
opts.C: A longer timeout on the tool call
opts.D: A retry loop with exponential backoff only

why: Duplicate delivery is a property of the transport, so the defense must live in the write path. Backoff reduces load but does not make a repeat harmless.
trap: D looks like reliability engineering but only changes retry timing.

stem: An MCP server exposes 40 tools; your workflow needs 3 of them. What is the architect's call?

opts.A: Expose all 40 and let the model choose
opts.B: Expose the 3, scoped to the credentials that workflow needs
opts.C: Expose all 40 but add a prompt instruction listing the 3
opts.D: Replace MCP with direct API calls

why: Least privilege applies to tool surface as much as to credentials, and a smaller surface also reduces tool-selection error and context cost.
trap: C confuses guidance with enforcement.

stem: Nightly, 200,000 documents need classification before a 6am report. Users are not waiting. Which design is strongest?

opts.A: Synchronous requests at maximum concurrency
opts.B: Message Batches with a results callback into the reporting pipeline
opts.C: A single request with all documents in context

why: Nothing interactive depends on the latency, so batching buys throughput and cost without a user-facing tradeoff.
trap: A invites rate-limit storms for no benefit.

stem: Your integration starts receiving 429s during a traffic spike. Which response is correct?

opts.A: Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
opts.B: Honor retry guidance, queue work, and smooth the burst
opts.C: Raise max_tokens to get more done per request

why: 429 is a capacity signal; the system must absorb it rather than amplify it into a retry storm.
trap: C and D confuse throughput limits with capability limits.

stem: A field-operations agent reads six independent systems, then writes one work order. How should the work be arranged?

opts.A: Serialize everything for predictability
opts.B: Parallelize the six reads, sequence the write after them
opts.C: Parallelize reads and write together
opts.D: Let the model decide ordering each run

why: Independent reads have no dependency, but the write depends on all of them; ordering is part of correctness, not a tuning preference.
trap: D makes a correctness property nondeterministic.

stem: A support corpus is 40 pages, changes twice a year, and nearly all of it is relevant to every question. What should the architect choose?

opts.A: Build a vector store with chunking and a reranker
opts.B: Put the corpus in context and cache the stable prefix
opts.C: Fine-tune a model on the corpus
opts.D: Call a live tool per question

why: A bounded, mostly-relevant, slow-changing corpus is the case where long context plus caching beats retrieval on both simplicity and operations.
trap: A is the reflex answer and adds a pipeline with no payoff here.

stem: An autonomous research agent has run 90 tool calls on one task and is still going. What was missing from the design?

opts.A: A more capable model
opts.B: Bounds on turns, tool calls, spend, and wall-clock time
opts.C: A larger context window

why: Autonomy without bounds is an unpriced liability; the loop needs stop conditions the application enforces.
trap: D relies on the model policing itself.

stem: Where should the authoritative status of an in-flight payment live?

opts.A: The conversation transcript
opts.B: The agent's summarized memory
opts.C: A transactional system of record

why: Durable business state belongs in a system built for persistence and consistency; model context is not a ledger.
trap: D is a copy, not a source of truth.

stem: Answer quality dropped after a release. Retrieval, prompt, model version, and a tool all changed. What does the architect do first?

opts.A: Roll back everything and move on
opts.B: Evaluate each layer separately against the golden set to attribute the regression
opts.C: Switch to a more capable model

why: A bad answer has a specific cause; attributing it to a layer is what makes the fix cheap and the next release safer.
trap: A restores service but leaves you unable to re-land any of the four changes.

stem: A team wants to raise an LLM-as-judge rubric to production scoring. What must exist first?

opts.A: A larger judge model
opts.B: Calibration of judge scores against human labels on a held-out set
opts.C: A lower temperature on the judge

why: A judge is itself a measured component; without agreement against human labels you cannot tell what its score means.
trap: A and C tune the judge without ever validating it.

stem: p50 latency is fine but users complain. p95 is four times p50. What should the architect instrument?

opts.A: Average latency over a longer window
opts.B: Per-span timing that separates retrieval, model, and tool time
opts.C: Total token spend per day
opts.D: Model accuracy on the golden set

why: Tail latency is usually one layer's problem; only per-span attribution tells you which one.
trap: A hides the tail rather than explaining it.

stem: A team has been rewording the system prompt for three weeks with no test set. What is the first correct action?

opts.A: Adopt a structured prompt template
opts.B: Define success criteria and a representative evaluation set
opts.C: Escalate to the most capable model

why: Without a measure, no change can be shown to be an improvement; evaluation precedes tuning.
trap: A feels like progress and still yields no signal.

stem: A retrieved vendor PDF contains text instructing the agent to email its tool credentials. The agent has an email tool. What design prevents harm?

opts.A: A system instruction telling Claude to ignore instructions in documents
opts.B: Retrieved content handled as data, plus credentials and send authority held outside the model's reach
opts.C: A prompt-injection classifier on the document
opts.D: Asking the model to flag suspicious documents

why: Injection is an authority problem: if the model cannot reach the credential or the send decision, the instruction has nothing to act on. Classifiers help but are not the boundary.
trap: A and D ask wishful prompting to do an architecture job.

stem: An underwriting agent is 78% confident a claim should be denied, and denial is final. What does the architecture require?

opts.A: Deny and log the confidence score
opts.B: Route to a human approver before the denial takes effect
opts.C: Retry with extended thinking until confidence exceeds 95%
opts.D: Deny, with a customer appeal path

why: Consequential and irreversible outcomes sit above the autonomy threshold regardless of the model's self-reported confidence.
trap: C treats a confidence number as a safety control.

stem: A regulator asks how a specific automated decision was reached eleven months ago. What must the system have recorded?

opts.A: The full prompt and response bodies for every request
opts.B: Immutable metadata: inputs' provenance, control outcomes, model identity and version, approvals, and timestamps
opts.C: Aggregate accuracy metrics for the period

why: Reconstruction needs decision metadata under a retention policy; storing raw bodies indefinitely creates its own privacy exposure.
trap: A conflates auditability with mass retention.

stem: A multi-tenant assistant must never surface one customer's documents to another. Where does that guarantee belong?

opts.A: In the system prompt, per request
opts.B: In identity, storage, retrieval scope, keys, and authorization, separated per tenant
opts.C: In a post-generation filter that redacts other tenants' names

why: Isolation is enforced by the data and authorization path; a model instruction is not a boundary and a filter runs after the leak has already happened.
trap: C is detection presented as prevention.

stem: A CFO asks whether the deployed agent is worth its cost. Which figure answers the question?

opts.A: Monthly token spend
opts.B: Cost per reviewed outcome the business accepts, against the manual baseline
opts.C: Average tokens per request

why: Stakeholders buy outcomes, not tokens. Unit economics must be denominated in the result a human accepts.
trap: A is the number teams report and the one that answers nothing on its own.

stem: Staging evidence was collected on build 9f21; production evidence on a rebuild of the same commit. What is the correct reading?

opts.A: Equivalent, since the commit is identical
opts.B: The earlier evidence no longer applies; one artifact digest must span every stage
opts.C: Acceptable if tests pass in both
opts.D: Acceptable if the rebuild is reproducible

why: Promotion evidence is cumulative for one artifact; a rebuild between stages breaks the chain the evidence pack asserts.
trap: A treats source identity as artifact identity.

stem: Every promotion gate for production is satisfied. What follows?

opts.A: The change deploys automatically
opts.B: The change is ready for human review; authorization is still a human act
opts.C: The change can skip the staging soak
opts.D: The rollback plan is no longer needed

why: Readiness is a measured state; authorization is a decision with an accountable owner. Conflating them removes the last human control.
trap: A is the efficiency argument that quietly deletes accountability.

stem: A model version you depend on will be retired in 90 days. What is the architect's lifecycle response?

opts.A: Pin the old version indefinitely
opts.B: Re-run the golden set against candidate versions, compare cost and quality, and schedule a migration with a rollback path
opts.C: Switch on the retirement date and monitor complaints
opts.D: Let each service choose its own replacement

why: Model migration is a release with measurable acceptance criteria and a revert path, not a date on a calendar.
trap: C makes customers the regression suite.

stem: A long system preamble and tool set is identical across 50,000 daily requests; the user turn varies. What is the cost move?

opts.A: Shorten the preamble by half
opts.B: Cache the stable prefix and keep volatile content last
opts.C: Route everything to a smaller model

why: A stable repeated prefix is exactly what prompt caching is for, and ordering determines how much of it can be reused.
trap: C trades quality for a saving caching gives you for free.

stem: Responses are being cut off mid-sentence. stop_reason is max_tokens. What is the correct diagnosis?

opts.A: The context window is exhausted
opts.B: The generation cap was reached; raise it or bound the output format
opts.C: The model is rate limited

why: max_tokens caps output only. The fix is a larger cap or a response contract that fits the budget.
trap: A is the standard confusion between input capacity and output cap.

stem: A triage classifier handles 99% of tickets correctly on a fast model; the ambiguous 1% causes expensive errors. Best architecture?

opts.A: Use the most capable model for all tickets
opts.B: Keep the fast model and escalate low-confidence or ambiguous cases
opts.C: Add every historical ticket to the prompt

why: Routing by complexity keeps the cost and latency of the common path while applying capability where it changes the outcome.
trap: A pays a blanket premium for a 1% problem.

stem: A downstream service requires an object with exactly claim_id, decision, and rationale. Which design is strongest?

opts.A: Instruct the model to always return valid JSON
opts.B: Schema-constrained structured output validated before the handoff
opts.C: Regex extraction from the prose response
opts.D: A few-shot prompt with three example objects

why: A machine boundary is enforced with a schema; prompt-shaped formatting is a tendency, not a contract.
trap: D works in demos and fails on the case you did not show it.

stem: A team writes 'never commit secrets' in CLAUDE.md and considers the control complete. What is wrong?

opts.A: The rule belongs in the README instead
opts.B: CLAUDE.md is guidance; a must-never rule needs a hook, permission, or CI check
opts.C: The rule should be repeated in every skill

why: Instruction files shape behavior; they do not enforce it. Deterministic enforcement is what makes a rule a control.
trap: C mistakes repetition for enforcement.

stem: A code-exploration task floods the main agent's context with search output and logs. What is the better structure?

opts.A: Raise the context window
opts.B: Delegate to a subagent with isolated context that returns only the conclusion
opts.C: Summarize the transcript every few turns
opts.D: Split the task across two sessions manually

why: Context isolation is the primary reason to use a subagent; parallelism is a secondary benefit.
trap: A pays for the noise instead of removing it.

stem: Four agents work the same repository at once and keep colliding on build and git state. What does the architect introduce?

opts.A: A shared lock file the agents are told to respect
opts.B: Separate worktrees so each agent has isolated filesystem and git state
opts.C: A single agent running the tasks sequentially

why: Isolation removes the conflict class rather than coordinating around it; blast-radius control is the general principle.
trap: A depends on every agent honoring a convention.

stem: A detailed 900-line deployment procedure is needed on roughly one task in twenty. Where does it belong?

opts.A: In CLAUDE.md so it is always available
opts.B: In a skill loaded on demand when the task calls for it
opts.C: In a hook that runs before every tool call
opts.D: In the system prompt of every request

why: On-demand loading keeps the always-on context small while leaving the procedure available where it matters.
trap: A taxes every unrelated turn with the same 900 lines.
